Why spend five minutes a day reviewing
More important than remembering is seeing yourself
We do so much every day, yet most of it blurs by bedtime. Reviewing isn’t writing a report; it’s pausing at the end of the day to look at who you were today.
Five minutes is enough. You don’t need to write well, just honestly. “Only learned 10 words today” is a valuable record too, because it shows you your real pace.
After a while, these scattered lines slowly join into a thread. You’ll see when you’re at your best, what you keep putting off, and which little things make you happy.
The real value of reviewing isn’t what you wrote on any one day; it’s that you start to know yourself.
Three questions for a good review
What I did, what I learned, what I’ll do tomorrow
If you don’t know what to write, try these three questions.
First, what did I do today? Just facts, no judgment, like “read 20 pages” or “tidied my desk”. Facts free you from the feeling that “I didn’t do anything today”.
Second, what did I learn? A piece of knowledge, or something about yourself, like “I can hardly focus after 3 pm”.
Third, what will I do tomorrow? Just one small thing, like “do the hardest task in the morning”.
Three questions, three sentences, and a full review is done.
Days you missed are worth recording too
Many people give up recording after a day they missed. That blank day feels like a stain, and they stop opening the app.
But reviewing isn’t attendance; it’s just a mirror. On a missed day, writing “Too tired today, resting first” is an honest review in itself.
Your rhythm will rise and fall, and that’s normal. What matters isn’t being perfect every day, but being willing to come back.
That’s why we don’t show streaks on cards. You can stop anytime, and start again anytime.
Fewer habits are easier to keep
Start with two or three small things
When starting out, many people add seven or eight cards at once and feel tired within days.
A better way is to start with the two or three small things you care about most. Once they feel natural, add new ones slowly.
If a card hasn’t lit up for a long time, don’t blame yourself. Maybe it just doesn’t fit you right now; delete it or rephrase it.
With fewer cards, each one you light up means more.
Ten minutes on the weekend for a weekly review
From daily dots to a weekly line
Xiaoman records the details; a weekly review shows the direction.
Find ten minutes on the weekend, open the “Summary” page and look at the week: which card shows up most? Which barely moved? Any feelings or problems that keep coming up in what you wrote?
Then make just one decision: what do I want to adjust next week? Maybe drop a card, or move something to a different time.
A good review makes things lighter, not heavier. If you feel tired, deleting a card is a good adjustment too.
Small tips on reviewing, each a few minutes’ read.
